items.content:
Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.5-Pro debuts at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Image Editing Leaderboard, and takes the #7 spot in Text to Image

MAI-Image-2.5-Pro is Microsoft AI's quality-focused image model, launched July 23 in preview on Microsoft Foundry. It joins MAI-Image-2.5 and MAI-Image-2.5-Flash in a family Microsoft positions as covering the quality-speed-cost curve, so builders can pick the point that fits their job. Pro sits at the quality end: Microsoft describes it as its highest-fidelity image model to date, aimed at hero imagery, detailed editing, and precise in-image text rendering.

In the Artificial Analysis Image Arena, MAI-Image-2.5-Pro debuts at #1 on the Image Editing Leaderboard, surpassing Reve 2.1, GPT Image 2, and Microsoft's own MAI-Image-2.5. In Text to Image it lands at #7.

On Microsoft Foundry, MAI-Image-2.5-Pro is priced per token: $5 per 1M text input tokens, $8 per 1M image input tokens, and $106 per 1M image output tokens, which works out to roughly $108.5 per 1k 1024x1024 images. That compares to $48 per 1k images for MAI-Image-2.5 and $20 per 1k for MAI-Image-2.5-Flash.

MAI-Image-2.5-Pro is available in preview on Microsoft Foundry across seven global-standard regions, and can be tried out in the MAI Playground.

Congratulations to @MicrosoftAI on the release!

See below for comparisons between MAI-Image-2.5-Pro and other leading models in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

Progress in open models is keeping Big AI labs up at night, and I'm here for it!

We have a brand ne...
items.content:
Progress in open models is keeping Big AI labs up at night, and I'm here for it!

We have a brand new open-weight multimodal model optimized for long-horizon tasks.

This model is really good at something: it can work on tasks that keep evolving over time.

• 280B total parameters, but only 16B active
• 512K context window
• Understands text, images, and audio
• Strong reasoning, coding, and tool use

But the best of all: the model learns and adapts to new information!

Imagine you start running an agent today to solve a problem, and while it's working, you get new information that changes the initial conditions, or you change your mind.

The agents you run today don't have issues with short tasks and goals that don't change, but reality is messy, and that makes it hard for long-horizon agents to succeed.

The new dots3-note Preview model introduces TEMPO.

TEMPO is a new reinforcement learning technique that lets the model periodically pause and critique its own progress.

Basically, from time to time, the agent asks itself: "Am I getting closer to the goal, or am I wasting my time?"

The same model switches between actor and critic. The actor works on the problem. The critic looks at the current state, reasons about how much progress it has made, and determines what should happen next.

TEMPO gives the model feedback along the way.

Progress in open models is keeping Big AI labs up at night, and I'm here for it!

We have a brand new open-weight multimodal model optimized for long-horizon tasks.

This model is really good at something: it can work on tasks that keep evolving over time.

• 280B total parameters, but only 16B active

• 512K context window

• Understands text, images, and audio

• Strong reasoning, coding, and tool use

But the best of all: the model learns and adapts to new information!

Imagine you start running an agent today to solve a problem, and while it's working, you get new information that changes the initial conditions, or you change your mind.

The agents you run today don't have issues with short tasks and goals that don't change, but reality is messy, and that makes it hard for long-horizon agents to succeed.

The new dots3-note Preview model introduces TEMPO.

TEMPO is a new reinforcement learning technique that lets the model periodically pause and critique its own progress.

Basically, from time to time, the agent asks itself: "Am I getting closer to the goal, or am I wasting my time?"

The same model switches between actor and critic. The actor works on the problem. The critic looks at the current state, reasons about how much progress it has made, and determines what should happen next.

TEMPO gives the model feedback along the way.

This is huge for any agent that can work on long-horizon tasks without wasting its time.

items.title: Deciding how large a language model should be, and how much text to train it on, usually comes down ...
items.content:
Deciding how large a language model should be, and how much text to train it on, usually comes down to a formula fitted on a batch of small, cheap training runs and then trusted well outside the range where it was fitted; the standard version, from the Chinchilla work, writes the final training error as one term that depends on model size plus a separate term that depends on the amount of data, which quietly assumes the two do nothing to each other.

In this paper from @AIatMeta, the authors check that assumption directly nearly 400 measured runs: they estimate how the error surface bends, and find that the quantity an additive formula forces to be exactly zero—how much the benefit of extra data changes when the model gets bigger—is not zero anywhere on their grid, and has a consistent sign, meaning growing both together buys more than growing either alone.

Their fix is to keep the two existing terms but raise their sum to one extra fitted power, which recovers the old formula when that power equals one and otherwise lets the two ingredients interact.

With that formula correction, prediction error on the held-out extremes of the grid falls by roughly half to two thirds, the formula can be fitted from cheap runs along the edges of the grid instead of the expensive interior, which means about ten times less compute.

I think the RAM score @xeophon and I made for ATOM work is a really solid metric. If I just rank by the top RAM scores @ 30days within our artifacts curation, all the models are really solid.

RAM score @ t= (model's cumulative downloads) @ t / (top-10 downloads for size class) @ t

RAM is essentially looking at a model's downloads at specific points in time (this case t is 30 days), relative to the downloads of the top 10 models of all time in that size bracket. A score of above 1 means it's on track to be a top 10 downloaded model at that size category. Imo most meaningful for 50B+ models.

Downloads alone normally isn't great on HuggingFace, but it's rare a large MoE gets a ton of adoption without being a solid model.

items.title: @TheEconomist .@TheEconomist  is a great publication, and I’ve learned a lot from it over the years....
items.content:
@TheEconomist .@TheEconomist  is a great publication, and I’ve learned a lot from it over the years. But I think it missed the mark with this article on @DAcemogluMIT.

Daron and I publicly and privately disagree on a number of important issues, most notably on the likely magnitude of AI’s productivity effects in the coming years. We’ve had many lengthy discussions about our differences, including as recently as last month.

That said, Daron is not merely one of the most intelligent, interesting, and hardworking economists I know. He is also a person of great integrity.

Since many people may form their impressions of him from this article or other public commentary, let me offer three anecdotes from my own experience.

1. In 2017, @tommmitchell  and I co-chaired a @theNASciences  committee on information technology and the workforce, bringing together a dozen leading scholars. Committee members were unpaid, and there was little extrinsic reward for doing more than the minimum. Everyone contributed, but unquestionably the person who worked hardest, and produced the most high-quality substantive material, was Daron. I came away enormously impressed by his seriousness and work ethic.

2. The article suggests that Daron’s stature may discourage others from criticizing him. That has not been my experience. I remember an MIT seminar where he presented an early version of his work on robots and employment. He was subjected to exceptionally tough criticism from colleagues and graduate students, especially over his instrumental variables and other aspects of his empirical strategy. It was one of the toughest seminars I can remember. Nobody was pulling punches. If anything, the criticism was blunter because everyone knew Daron was perfectly capable of handling it.

3. Along with @professor_ajay, @akorinek, and @testingham, I helped lead the recent “We Must Act Now” statement on AI (https://t.co/BjiX5fGGhJ). One of the first people we approached was Daron precisely because he had disagreed with me about AI capabilities and their likely economic effects. Daron and I went back and forth over the detailed wording for about a week. We ultimately found common ground. In the process, I was reminded of both his openness to new data and his attention to detail.

The Economist correctly highlights some important weaknesses in the economics profession. It should certainly scrutinize the work of prominent economists, presenting arguments and counterarguments.

In my view, what undermined their case was the article’s  shift from criticizing his arguments to innuendo about Daron's personality. The suggestion that economists are unwilling to challenge him does not match what I have observed over 3 decades of knowing him.

Criticize Daron’s ideas and conclusions, as I often do. But the personal insinuations struck me as unfair.

A self-improving agent can look better in validation and still fail to improve where it counts.

Tes...
items.content:
A self-improving agent can look better in validation and still fail to improve where it counts.

Tested GPT-5.6 Sol as an optimizer for two already-engineered SWE-bench agent harnesses.

The optimizer read failures, diagnosed recurring problems, and rewrote the worker’s instructions.

One edit looked like an obvious success. It doubled its validation score.

Then it hit tasks the optimizer had never seen.

No net improvement.

Another edit looked much less convincing during validation, yet performed better on the sealed test.

That changes the problem.

> How do you separate real improvement from a lucky gate?
> How do you catch regressions hidden behind a higher score?
> How much evidence should an agent need before its own edit becomes permanent?

The edits did change how the agent approached problems. They pushed it toward different code paths and different fixes.

But a better-looking validation result did not reliably tell which behavior should ship.

We're inviting science communicators in AI to submit proposals to teach an emerging technical concept. Ten teams on what you do instead of trusting the model:

- A member mentioning self harm or an acute emergency is routed to 911 by code that runs above the model. The model never even sees the turn
- You cannot A/B test on patients and you cannot roll back a phone call. So an LLM plays the patient first, and real patients rated the simulated one more human in three of four blind sets
- 31 models run on every Hippocratic call: one leads, 30 specialists decide turn by turn whether to speak. At 10,000 calls a day, a 1 percent error rate is 100 wrong appointments, daily
- Anterior cannot keep medical records even anonymized, so 90 percent of its eval data is generated backward from policy decision trees. Clinicians spot the fakes about 60 percent of the time
- ECRI, the patient safety group hospitals use to rank risk, named AI chatbot misuse the number one health technology hazard of 2026. These ten talks are what shipping against that looks like

items.content:
Most agents don't work. Period.

I make a living testing AI applications, and around 80% of the demos I've seen don't last a single day in the hands of a real user.

Creating a production-ready agent is way more complex than people think. Your agent needs to do all of this:

• Manage context across long-running tasks
• Call tools in the right order
• Delegate work to subagents
• Stop for human approval before doing something consequential
• Execute code in a sandbox
• Leave a trace you can inspect when things go wrong

That infrastructure is what we call the "agent harness", and implementing a good one is hard.

99% of people should start off with a good foundation harness instead of reinventing the wheel.

Check out TrueForge, an open-source, vendor-neutral agent harness you can start using right now. The @truefoundry team that's behind this project is partnering with me on this post.

You can use models from different providers and route each task to the model that makes sense.

For context, in a 14-task enterprise-agent benchmark, TrueForge matched Claude Managed Agents running Opus 4.8 while costing ~30% less on the same Opus model, and up to ~75% less when TrueForge routed the work to GLM-5.2.

Here is what you get when you use TrueForge:

1. Open-source (MIT license), so you can just host it on your own infrastructure.

2. Vendor-neutral, so you can use any model that fits each task.

3. The ability to orchestrate tools, manage context, run subagents, and have human-in-the-loop checkpoints.

items.content:
This Unitree robot is nine feet tall, weighs half a ton, and has a cockpit in its chest that a human can climb into.

The GD01 walks on two legs or four, and costs $650,000.

When TIME visited Unitree’s Hangzhou headquarters, their founder Wang Xingxing wouldn’t get in or even turn it on, because “It might not be safe,” he said.

That’s a striking thing to hear from the biggest humanoid maker in the world, a company shipping over 5,500 units last year.

It just filed for a $6B IPO, and has pushed its flagship G1 down to $13,500 by building its own actuators, the motors that make up most of a humanoid’s cost.

But the numbers underneath tell a stranger story. Only 9% of its humanoid sales go to real industrial work.

74% go to universities and developers, meaning the industry is largely selling robots to people trying to build better robots.

Hardware is racing ahead. The software that makes these machines genuinely useful is still the hard part.

My brother once called me about a used Model S he found for $35,000 in Virginia. He never thought he would be able to afford one. I wrote at the time that once you go electric you never go back to gas.

I thought about that call reading this breakdown.

On Monday I wrote about the 5% toll gateways quietly take out of every token, and said somebody had just taken it to zero. This is what happened next.

903 companies applied to a 0% AI gateway in 48 hours. The headline is the $13.3 million. The real story is the 400+ small teams spending a few hundred dollars a month on tokens.

The toll was never a crisis for these teams. It was a tax they assumed was permanent, the way stock trades cost $40 until one day they cost nothing.

Once somebody shows you the toll was optional, you never pay it again. Ever.

items.content:
@DarshanG_ @OpenRouter @Etched @ivanburazin @GroqInc @OpenPipeAI I don’t really have a process for figuring out what the future is going to look like. It’s the one thing I’ve always just kind of been able to do pretty well, and haven’t really been able to teach anyone. A lot of it really is just gut feeling, combined with some high-level data.

One mistake I see people making is getting too deep into the weeds, they usually find a million things that will break the overall thesis. Everything has roadblocks, you’re mostly looking at the incentives to build towards the future and break those, and the high-level physics of the thing (i’m not even close to an expert on this so I just read a lot and try to form my own opinions, + gut)

I do have a very small fund, but I don’t really have an interest right now in running a much larger one. I think part of why I’m good at this is that it’s not a full-time job for me. I don’t screen companies. When I find something I want to invest in, I reach out. That’s pretty much it. If I were screening companies all day, I would probably be doing much worse.

Plus, I just really like building and sharing what I learn. A big part of my personal goal right now is just to help as many people as possible understand what’s coming down the pipe with AI. Feels like our moral imperative at this point and very few people are doing it in a way that’s understandable to the average person.

I could probably make more money investing, raise a huge fund, fees, carry, etc., but I think right now, the world needs a clear understanding of what is happening, much more than I need some carry lol. And no one seems to be doing that well (SV folks love to talk in jargon).

That said, if anyone wants to convince me to start a big fund, happy to chat about it. But I don’t like your odds. :)

Sorry if this is confusingly worded, it’s late and I’ve had a very long day

Everything has roadblocks, you’re mostly looking at the incentives to build towards the future and break those, and the high-level physics of the thing (i’m not even close to an expert on this so I just read a lot and try to form my own opinions, + gut)

I do have a very small fund, but I don’t really have an interest right now in running a much larger one. I think part of why I’m good at this is that it’s not a full-time job for me. I don’t screen companies. When I find something I want to invest in, I reach out. That’s pretty much it. If I were screening companies all day, I would probably be doing much worse.

Plus, I just really like building and sharing what I learn. A big part of my personal goal right now is just to help as many people as possible understand what’s coming down the pipe with AI. Feels like our moral imperative at this point and very few people are doing it in a way that’s understandable to the average person.

I could probably make more money investing, raise a huge fund, fees, carry, etc., but I think right now, the world needs a clear understanding of what is happening, much more than I need some carry lol. And no one seems to be doing that well (SV folks love to talk in jargon).

That said, if anyone wants to convince me to start a big fund, happy to chat about it. But I don’t like your odds. :)

Sorry if this is confusingly worded, it’s late and I’ve had a very long day
